title: Hashing
html:
Hashing turns a key into an array index with a hash function, so that search, insert and delete all run in O(1) on average. It is the engine behind every dictionary, set, cache and database index you will ever use.

Hashing — a technique that maps keys from a large universe (all integers, all strings …) into a small array called the hash table using a hash function h(key) → 0 … m-1. The slot h(key) is where the key is stored and where it is looked up again.

Universe of keys
→
Hash function h(key)
→
Index 0 … m-1
→
Hash table slot
OperationAverageWorst caseWhy
search(key)O(1)O(n)Compute h(key), look in that slot. Worst case: every key collided into the same slot.
insert(key)O(1)O(n)Same slot computation; the worst case is a full probe sequence or a long chain.
delete(key)O(1)O(n)Find the key as in search, then unlink / mark it.
Key point

The O(1) is average and relies on a good hash function and a table that is not overfull (low load factor, see below). A bad hash function degrades a hash table to a linked list.

What hashing is good for — and what it is not

Dictionaries and sets

Language containers: Python dict/set, C++ unordered_map, Java HashMap, JS Map.

Database indexing

Hash indexes answer WHERE id = 42 without scanning the table.

Cryptography

SHA-256 and friends are hash functions designed so that collisions are infeasible to find.

Caches

A cache maps a request key to a stored response in O(1) — memoisation, CPU caches, CDNs.

Symbol tables

Compilers and interpreters look up every identifier by name in a hash table.

Routers

A router maps a destination address to an output port with a hash lookup.

Watch out

Hashing is not the right tool when you need order: finding the closest value, the k-th smallest, a sorted traversal, or prefix searches (use a Trie) and range queries (use a balanced BST / sorted array). A hash table scatters keys deliberately, so neighbouring keys end up far apart.

Direct address table

Suppose there are at most 1000 keys and every key is an integer between 0 and 999. The simplest O(1) structure is a boolean (or value) array of size 1000 where the key is the index: table[key] = true inserts, table[key] searches, table[key] = false deletes.

Time O(1) per operationSpace O(size of key universe)
Avoid

The direct address table cannot handle large or non-integer keys: 10-digit phone numbers would need a 10-billion-slot array, and strings have no natural index at all. Hashing fixes this by compressing the key universe into a small range 0 … m-1.

Hash functions

A hash function h converts a key into a slot index. A good one has four properties:

  1. Deterministic — the same key must always map to the same slot, or we could never find it again.
  2. In range — produces values in 0 … m-1 where m is the table size.
  3. Fast — O(1) for integers and O(len) for a string of length len.
  4. Uniform — spreads keys evenly across the slots, so that chains and probe sequences stay short.
Key typeTypical hash functionNote
Integerh(key) = key % mChoose m prime and not close to a power of 2, so patterns in the keys (even numbers, multiples of 10) do not pile up in a few slots.
StringWeighted (polynomial) sum: h = (h · 31 + c) % m over the charactersPlain sum of character codes is bad: "abc", "bca", "cab" would all collide. The weight makes position matter.
AnyUniversal hashing: pick h at random from a family of functions at start-upNo fixed input can be adversarially chosen to collide, because the attacker does not know which function was picked.
Time O(len) per stringSpace O(1)
Key point

Java's String.hashCode() is exactly this polynomial with base 31 (without the modulo); Python and JavaScript engines use randomised variants so that attackers cannot pre-compute colliding keys.

Collisions and how to handle them

Collision — two different keys hashing to the same slot: h(k1) == h(k2) with k1 != k2. With more possible keys than slots, collisions are unavoidable (pigeonhole principle) — a hash table design is mostly a decision about what to do when they happen.

Perfect hashing

If all keys are known in advance (keywords of a programming language, a fixed set of country codes) a collision-free function can be constructed offline. Not possible for dynamic data.

Chaining

Each slot holds a list of all keys that hashed there. The table never fills up.

Open addressing

All keys live inside the array. On a collision, probe other slots in a fixed order until an empty one is found: linear probing, quadratic probing or double hashing.

Chaining

The table is an array of m list heads. insert appends to the list at h(key), search and delete walk that one list only. With h(key) = key % 7 and the keys 50, 21, 58, 17, 15, 49, 56, 22, 23, 25:

Performance. Let m be the number of slots and n the number of keys. The load factor α = n / m is the expected chain length under uniform hashing, so:

expected search / delete time = O(1 + α) — O(1) to hash, O(α) to walk the chain

Keeping α bounded by a constant (Java's HashMap rehashes at α = 0.75) makes every operation O(1) on average. Chains can be stored in any of these:

Chain structureProsCons
Linked listO(1) insert at head, no resizingPoor cache locality, one pointer per key
Dynamic array (vector, ArrayList, Python list)Cache friendly, simpleDelete from the middle shifts elements (chains are short, so it hardly matters)
Self-balancing BST (AVL, Red-Black)Worst case per chain drops to O(log n) — Java 8+ HashMap switches a bucket to a tree when it grows past 8 entriesHeavier nodes, more code
Example

Input: buckets = 7; insert 70, 71, 9, 56, 72; delete 56; search 9, 93
Output: 9 → true, 93 → false

Time O(1 + α) average, O(n) worstSpace O(n + m)

Load factor and rehashing

Load factor α — n / m — the number of stored keys divided by the number of slots. It measures how full the table is and directly controls the cost of every operation.

Rehashing: when α crosses a threshold (typically 0.75 for chaining, 0.5 for open addressing), allocate a new table about twice as large and re-insert every key with the new h — the slot of a key depends on m, so the old positions are useless. One rehash costs O(n), but it happens only after O(n) cheap inserts, so insertion stays amortised O(1).

SchemeExpected successful searchExpected unsuccessful search / insertMust keep
ChainingO(1 + α)O(1 + α)α bounded by a constant (any value works, even α > 1)
Open addressingabout 1/α · ln(1/(1-α))about 1 / (1 - α)α < 1, in practice α ≤ 0.5 … 0.7
Key point

Read the open-addressing formula at α = 0.5: an unsuccessful search probes about 2 slots; at α = 0.9 about 10. Performance degrades sharply as the table fills, which is why open-addressing tables resize early.

Open addressing — linear probing

In open addressing there are no chains: every key lives in the array itself, so the number of slots must be >= the number of keys. On a collision we probe — try other slots in a fixed sequence until an empty one appears. Because all data is in one contiguous array, this is very cache friendly.

linear probing: hash(key, i) = (h(key) + i) % m for i = 0, 1, 2, …

With m = 7, h(key) = key % 7 and the keys 50, 51, 49, 16, 56, 15, 19:

Searching

Compute h(key) and compare. If the slot holds another key, keep moving to the next slot. Stop with not found when you hit an empty slot or come back to the start index.

Deleting

Never simply empty the slot. An empty slot ends every search passing through it, so keys that were probed past this slot would become unreachable. Instead write a special DELETED marker: search skips over it, insert may reuse it.

Inserting

Probe from h(key) until an empty or deleted slot; fail if the table is full or the key already exists (search first).

Primary clustering — the phenomenon where keys that hash to the same or nearby slots form long runs of occupied slots. Any key hashing into a cluster lands at its end and makes it longer, so clusters grow faster and faster — search, insert and delete all degrade towards O(n). Linear probing suffers from it most.

Quadratic probing and double hashing

Both break clusters by making the probe sequence depend on something other than +1:

SchemeProbe sequenceClusteringGuarantee
Linear probing(h(key) + i) % mPrimary clusteringAlways finds a free slot if one exists
Quadratic probing(h(key) + i²) % mSecondary clustering (keys with the same h still share a sequence)Guaranteed to find a free slot only if m is prime and α < 0.5
Double hashing(h1(key) + i · h2(key)) % mNone — different keys with the same h1 almost always get different step sizesFinds a free slot if one exists when h2(key) is relatively prime to m (e.g. m prime and h2(key) = 1 + key % (m-1))

Double hashing distributes keys more uniformly than linear and quadratic probing and is the closest practical approximation to the uniform hashing assumption behind the 1 / (1 - α) analysis. The insert routine from the notes:

1
Reject a full table
If n == m return an error — open addressing cannot store more keys than slots.
2
Compute the start and the step
probe = h1(key), offset = h2(key).
3
Walk the sequence
While table[probe] is occupied: probe = (probe + offset) % m.
4
Store
table[probe] = key.
Example

Input: m = 7, h1 = key % 7, h2 = 1 + key % 6; insert 50, 51, 49, 16, 56, 15, 19
Output: slots 0..6: 49 50 51 56 19 16 15

Time O(1 / (1 - α)) expected per insertSpace O(m)
Pitfall

h2(key) must never be 0 (the probe would stay in place forever) and must be relatively prime to m, otherwise the sequence visits only a fraction of the slots and can miss free ones. m prime with h2 = 1 + key % (m - 1) satisfies both.

Implementation of open addressing

A complete linear-probing table with the DELETED marker. Empty slots are -1, deleted slots -2; keys are assumed non-negative. insert refuses duplicates and reuses deleted slots; search skips deleted slots and stops at an empty one.

Example

Input: capacity = 7; insert 70, 71, 9, 56, 72; delete 9; search 9, 56; insert 56 again
Output: search 9 → false, search 56 → true, insert 56 → false (duplicate)

Time O(1) average, O(n) worstSpace O(m)
Pitfall

Walk through search 56 after delete 9: h(56) = 0 → slot 0 holds 70, slot 1 holds 71, slot 2 is DELETED (skip!), slot 3 holds 56 → found. Had delete emptied slot 2 instead, the search would have stopped there and reported 56 as missing even though it is in the table.

Chaining vs open addressing

ChainingOpen addressing
Table full?Never — chains simply growYes; resizing becomes mandatory
Sensitivity to hash functionLow — a poor function only lengthens chainsHigh — clustering needs extra care
Cache performancePoor: chain nodes are scattered in memoryGood: everything is in one array
Extra spaceOne link pointer per keyEmpty slots must be kept (α well below 1) to achieve the same performance
DeletionUnlink from the chainNeeds the DELETED marker
Unsuccessful search cost1 + α1 / (1 - α)

Problem: frequencies of array elements

Example

Input: arr = [10, 12, 10, 15, 10, 20, 12, 12]
Output: 10 3 / 12 3 / 15 1 / 20 1

Naive approach — for every element, skip it if it appeared earlier (so each value is printed once), otherwise count its later occurrences. Two nested passes make it O(n²) with O(1) extra space.

Time O(n²)Space O(1)
Idea

Efficient solution — one pass with a hash map from value to count: freq[x] += 1 is an O(1) average update, so the whole array is processed in O(n). Hash maps iterate in an unspecified order, so the keys are sorted before printing to make the output deterministic.

Time O(n) average (O(n log n) with the final sort)Space O(n)
Key point

If the output must follow first appearance order instead, Python dict and JavaScript Map already preserve insertion order; use LinkedHashMap in Java and keep a separate vector of first-seen keys in C++.

Interview Q&A

Why is a hash table O(1) only on average?

The hash function could map every key to the same slot; then every operation walks a chain (or probe sequence) of length n. With a uniform hash function and bounded load factor the expected chain length is α, a constant, giving O(1) expected time. Balanced BSTs guarantee O(log n) in the worst case, which is why they are preferred when adversarial inputs or hard latency bounds matter.

What is the load factor and what happens when it gets too high?

α = n / m, keys per slot. Chaining cost grows linearly as 1 + α; open addressing grows as 1 / (1 - α) and explodes near 1. Libraries rehash into a table about twice as big when α crosses a threshold (0.75 in Java's HashMap), re-inserting all keys — O(n) once, amortised O(1) per insert.

Why can't you just empty a slot when deleting from an open-addressing table?

Searches stop at the first empty slot. Keys that were inserted past the deleted slot (because it was occupied at the time) would no longer be reachable. A DELETED tombstone keeps searches going while letting inserts reuse the slot. Too many tombstones slow down searches, so tables rehash when live + deleted slots get numerous.

Chaining or open addressing — which would you choose?

Chaining when deletions are frequent, the load is unpredictable or the hash function is mediocre: it never fills and degrades gracefully. Open addressing when memory locality matters and keys are small (ints): it avoids pointer chasing and allocation, which is why high-performance tables (Google's SwissTable, Python's dict) use open addressing with careful probing.

Why should the table size be prime for modulo hashing?

key % m with m = 2^k keeps only the low k bits of the key, so keys differing only in higher bits collide. Keys that are multiples of a common factor of m land in a fraction of the slots. A prime m shares no factors with typical key patterns and spreads them over all slots.
